newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Protesters hate Serbia's ruling couple.
newsitem.headline: Protesters hate Serbia's ruling couple.

text.p: It was a sure sign Serbia's president was facing a serious crisis when his powerful wife failed to publish her column this month.
"There must be trouble if there's no column," said one Belgrade journalist.

The column, which normally appears every second week on Fridays in a weekly magazine called Duga (Rainbow), is treated as an oracle for the ruling socialists and diplomats watching for President Slobodan Milosevic's next move.
Diplomats say all roads to Milosevic pass through gates guarded by his wife, Mirjana Markovic.
"The word is if you fall out with Mira, you're finished," said one diplomat.
Isolated and aloof, they are fiercely loyal to each other and have stayed silent throughout a wave of street protests that have shaken the country.
Poll fraud set off three weeks of demonstrations last month but the real target of popular outrage is clearly fixed on the ruling couple.
The protesters, for whom Markovic provokes even more anger than her autocratic husband, parade effigies of Milosevic dressed in prison garb and his wife with a devil's tail.
Critics draw parallels to Nicolae and Elena Ceausescu and other despotic couples whose arrogance grew as their own people descended into misery.
Since his rise to power nine years ago, no personality in Milosevic's circle has been so hated as his wife, a sociology professor and avowed Marxist.
Milosevic once shielded her from the public spotlight but she became more and more prominent since he started to ditch nationalist rhetoric to remake himself as "peacemaker".
Wearing a flower in her hair and less-than-fashionable attire over a plump figure, she can be heard often on state TV speaking in a high-pitched voice about the inevitable triumph of "the Left".
Her party, the Yugoslav United Left, promotes nostalgia for old-fashioned Yugoslav communism but its members include wealthy managers keen on keeping good "connections".
During peace negotiations with Milosevic last year, Western diplomats say only his wife was allowed to interrupt.
"He is almost completely isolated. He doesn't have a circle of capable advisers around him," said one diplomat. "Only his wife has access."
Many members of the socialist party blame this month's debacle at the polls on a coalition with Markovic's party.
During the election campaign, the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition found that bashing "Mira" was a big crowd pleaser.
Forsaking nationalism, Milosevic and his wife have returned to slogans of their youth when they met as ambitious members of the Communist Party.
But the workers are hungry and the factories are idle.
Songs about World War Two anti-Nazi partisans sound hollow from the same leadership that plunged the country into a war to build a Greater Serbia.
The party elite have grown rich, writing their own rules for a government cartel while pensioners struggle to pay for bread.
Angry demonstrators in Belgrade, who accuse the socialists of vote-rigging and rampant corruption, chant "thieves" and "red bandits" as they march past government buildings.

"I hope they all burn in hell, because there is only one God and he will judge them on their record, and that record is pretty bad." said a student protester called Vesna. "Take a look around you and see what they've done."
